Predict time-reallocation effects

Source: R/predict_realloc.R
predict_realloc.Rd

Estimates the effect of reallocating time between the parts of a composition, from a comp_iv() fit. Each estimate is the contrast of the model's linear predictor between a reallocated composition and a reference composition, computed by emmeans. It is back-transformed to the response scale: an odds, hazard, rate or risk ratio for a ratio-scale model, and a mean difference for a linear one.

Usage

predict_realloc(
  object,
  delta,
  from = NULL,
  to = NULL,
  scheme = c("one-to-one", "one-to-all"),
  realloc = NULL,
  reference = NULL,
  type = c("relative", "absolute"),
  at = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  on_invalid = c("na", "omit", "error")
)

Arguments

object

A comp_iv / timecoda_fit from comp_iv().

delta

Time to reallocate, in the composition's closure units: a number or vector of numbers, each applied to every from/to pair (a negative value moves time the other way). Ignored in custom mode (when realloc is supplied), where each scenario has its own signed changes.

from, to

Character vectors of part names defining the reallocations. For scheme = "one-to-one" (the default), they name the donor (from) and receiver (to) parts and default to all ordered pairs. If given, they are matched elementwise (scalars recycled). For scheme = "one-to-all", supply only one of them. Each part it names is a focal part in turn, and the other side is implicitly all remaining parts (see scheme).

scheme

How time is reallocated. "one-to-one" (default) moves delta closure units directly between the from and to parts. "one-to-all" moves delta closure units between a single focal part \(f\) and all the remaining parts, in proportion to their values in the reference composition \(r\). Remaining part \(j\) changes by \(\mp \delta \, r_j / \sum_{k \ne f} r_k\), and the remaining parts keep their ratios to one another. With to = "MVPA" the focal part gains time from the rest, and with from = "MVPA" it gives time to the rest. With neither, every part is used as the focal receiver in turn. The implicit "all remaining parts" side is labelled "(rest)" in the from/to output column.

realloc

Optional custom multi-part reallocation, in the style of Dumuid et al. (2022) "Your best day". In place of a directed from/to pair, give a signed change per part, in the composition's closure units. The changes are added to the reference composition, which is then re-closed. For example, c(SPT = 30, SB = -15, LPA = -15) moves 30 minutes into sleep, taken 15 each from SB and LPA. Accepts (1) a named numeric vector (one scenario), (2) a list of named numeric vectors (several scenarios), or (3) a data frame with one column per part and one row per scenario. Every scenario must name known parts, sum to zero (to within 1e-8; a closed reallocation), and hold at least one positive and one negative entry. Parts left unnamed are held at their reference value. Custom mode is mutually exclusive with from, to and scheme. type, at, by and on_invalid apply as for a directed reallocation, and a multinomial fit still gives one row set per outcome category.

reference

Optional named numeric vector (or one-row data frame) giving the composition to anchor the reallocations at: one strictly positive value per part, summing to the fit's composition total. The default (NULL) uses the sample's closed geometric mean, stored in the fit.

type

"relative" (default) contrasts each reallocated composition against the reference; "absolute" returns the predicted response at each composition. "cox", "coxme", "clm", "clmm" and "mblogit" fits support "relative" only.

at

Optional named list of covariate values at which to evaluate. Each covariate that interacts with the composition must be pinned by at or split by by. Covariates not in at are averaged over in the usual emmeans way.

by

Optional name of a factor or character covariate, to compute the reallocation per group. The contrast is evaluated once at each level present in the fitted data. The result gains a column named after the covariate, holding the level (e.g., one odds ratio per sex for a moderated effect). When the fit was built with a factor moderator (see comp_iv()) and at does not pin it, by defaults to that moderator. at and by cannot name the same covariate. Pin numeric covariates with at instead.

conf_level

Confidence level for the intervals.

on_invalid

What to do when a reallocation drives a part to zero or below: "na" (default) keeps the rows but returns NA estimates for them; "omit" drops those rows; "error" aborts.

Value

A realloc object, a tibble with columns from, to, delta, estimate, std.error, df, conf.low, conf.high, statistic and p.value (statistic and p.value only for type = "relative"). std.error is on the scale of estimate. For a ratio effect it is the standard error of the ratio itself, as emmeans reports it on the response scale; the standard error of the log ratio is not returned. For type = "absolute", the first row is the reference composition (from, to = NA, delta = 0). A by grouping adds a column named after the covariate, and a multinomial fit adds response_level, one row set per non-reference outcome category. In custom mode, each scenario's from and to are compact, comma-separated signed part strings (e.g., from = "LPA -15, SB -15", to = "SPT +30"), and delta is the scenario's total time moved, in closure units. summary() builds the summary table from it. The fit metadata that method needs is stored as attributes, among them units, the composition's unit label (NULL when none was declared).

Details

The reference and every reallocated composition are converted to the fit's ILR coordinates and evaluated as their own emmeans reference grids, averaged over the covariates. Each reallocated row is contrasted with the reference row on the link scale, \(\eta(x_{\mathrm{realloc}}) - \eta(x_{\mathrm{ref}})\), with a delta-method standard error, and back-transformed with type = "response". Every row is its own Wald test, with no multiplicity adjustment across rows. The estimates do not depend on the ILR basis when the model is linear in the coordinates or holds their full quadratic (ilr()). A row with delta = 0 contrasts the reference with itself and is reported as the reference value (1 for a ratio, 0 for a difference), with a zero standard error, NA degrees of freedom and no test.

Without composition-by-covariate interactions, the covariates cancel in the contrast and a relative estimate does not depend on them. With such interactions the contrast is covariate-conditional. Every interacting covariate must then be pinned with at, or the contrast evaluated per level with by; the call aborts naming any covariate left unpinned. On a fit built with include_total = TRUE, every composition is evaluated with t_total held at the fit's total_ref. A reallocation then changes the shares at a constant total, and the total cancels from a relative contrast.

type = "absolute" returns the predicted response at each composition instead of a contrast. It is not available for "cox", "coxme", "clm", "clmm" or "mblogit" fits. These have no single absolute-response scale: Cox leaves its baseline hazard unestimated, and ordinal and multinomial predictions are per outcome category.

The df column holds the degrees of freedom emmeans computes for the fit, and the per-part table of summary() uses the same degrees of freedom. For an "lmer" fit, the default is the Kenward-Roger approximation through pbkrtest. The Satterthwaite approximation through lmerTest is used when it is selected with emmeans::emm_options(lmer.df =), or when pbkrtest cannot be used (absent, disabled, or more observations than emmeans::emm_options(pbkrtest.limit =)). Both packages are optional, and when neither can be used the degrees of freedom are Inf (asymptotic). For "glmer", "cox", "coxme" and "rlmer" fits the degrees of freedom are Inf (robustlmm reports none), and for "lmrob" fits they are the residual degrees of freedom.

A reallocation that drives any part to zero or below has no composition to evaluate. By default (on_invalid = "na"), such a row is kept with NA estimates. A sweep over many pairs or deltas then still returns every feasible row, and the printed summary gives the number of rows with no estimate. "omit" drops those rows instead, and "error" aborts the whole call on the first one.

The reference composition and "isotemporal substitution"

The reference argument sets the composition every reallocation starts from, and the contrast is computed the same way at any reference. The default, the cohort's geometric-mean day, suits population-typical questions. A day supplied by the user, such as a guideline schedule or one person's day, suits scenario questions. In the compositional time-use literature this prediction is compositional isotemporal substitution (Dumuid et al. 2019). The traditional leave-one-out isotemporal substitution model (Mekary et al. 2009) is a different regression parameterization, and no choice of reference reproduces it. vignette("predicting-reallocations") compares the two.

References

Dumuid, D., Pedišić, Ž., Stanford, T. E., et al. (2019). The compositional isotemporal substitution model: A method for estimating changes in a health outcome for reallocation of time between sleep, physical activity and sedentary behaviour. Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 28(3), 846-857. doi:10.1177/0962280217737805

Mekary, R. A., Willett, W. C., Hu, F. B., & Ding, E. L. (2009). Isotemporal substitution paradigm for physical activity epidemiology and weight change. American Journal of Epidemiology, 170(4), 519-527. doi:10.1093/aje/kwp163

Dumuid, D., Olds, T., Wake, M., et al. (2022). "Your best day": An interactive app to translate how time reallocations within a 24-hour day are associated with health measures. PLOS ONE, 17(9), e0272343. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0272343

Kenward, M. G., & Roger, J. H. (1997). Small sample inference for fixed effects from restricted maximum likelihood. Biometrics, 53(3), 983-997. doi:10.2307/2533558

See also

comp_iv() to fit the model this consumes; summary.realloc() for the summary table; plot_realloc() for the continuous sweep figure; optimal_composition() to search for the best-predicted composition instead of a directed transfer.

Other reallocation and prediction: optimal_composition(), plot_realloc(), summary.realloc()

Examples

cd <- declare_composition(timeuse, c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB", "SPT"),
                          closure = 1440)
fit <- comp_iv(cd, outcome = "obesity", model = "glm", family = "binomial")
predict_realloc(fit, delta = 30, from = "SB", to = "MVPA")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   from  to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 SB    MVPA     30    0.620    0.0561   Inf    0.519     0.740     -5.29
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>

# Proportional reallocation: add 30 min to MVPA, taken from the rest of the
# day in proportion to its composition.
predict_realloc(fit, delta = 30, scheme = "one-to-all", to = "MVPA")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   from   to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr>  <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (rest) MVPA     30    0.639    0.0569   Inf    0.536     0.761     -5.03
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>

# Custom multi-part reallocation ("best-day" style): add 30 min to SPT,
# taken 15 each from SB and LPA.
predict_realloc(fit, realloc = c(SPT = 30, SB = -15, LPA = -15))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   from         to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr>        <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 LPA -15, SB… SPT …    30    0.961    0.0367   Inf    0.892      1.04     -1.03
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>

# Anchor the same transfer at a chosen day instead of the cohort mean.
predict_realloc(fit, delta = 30, from = "SB", to = "MVPA",
                reference = c(MVPA = 30, LPA = 240, SB = 660, SPT = 510))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   from  to    delta estimate std.error    df conf.low conf.high statistic
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 SB    MVPA     30    0.632    0.0548   Inf    0.533     0.749     -5.30
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: p.value <dbl>
